items.article_search_text: Oscar Piastri has lost his points finish in the Mexican Grand Prix after the stewards penalised him for a collision. 2nd November 2026, 0:10 2nd November 2026, 9:05 | Written by Keith Collantine Advert | Become a Supporter & go ad-free The McLaren driver tangled with Arvid Lindblad while trying to overtake the Racing Bulls driver. The stewards issued the McLaren driver a 10-second time penalty which drops him from seventh place to 15th. The stewards ruled Piastri was not entitled to be given racing room when he tried to pass Lindblad on the outside of the corner and could have avoided the collision. “On the approach to turn one the driver of car 81 [Piastri] attempted an overtake on the outside of car 41 [Lindblad],” the stewards explained. “Car 81 was never fully alongside car 41 so was not able to claim the right to the corner. “Through turn one, the driver of car 41 defended his position by releasing the brakes however [did] not force car 81 off the track, allowing racing room on the outside – which he is not required to do. “The stewards determined that the collision could have been avoided if the driver of car 81 had moved further to the left after turn one, even if this involved leaving the track prior to turn two.” Speaking before the stewards issued their decision Piastri said there was little he could have done to avoid the contact. “I obviously need to look back at it more,” he said, “but from in the car, I went to go up the inside of turn one Arvid moved very late and so I kind of ended up on the outside because I was avoiding him. And then from that point onwards, I tried to go around the outside. “He pushed me pretty wide and I was trying to back out and you where we made contact was well before the corner actually happened. So from my side of things I really didn’t have anywhere else to go.” Did the stewards issue the correct penalty? Cast your vote below and have your say in the comments. View all posts by Keith Collantine Hilarious how this track with these cars is so awful for overtaking that Piastri could defend his position even with the damage he collected. He clearly had no pace, but still it was enough to defend his position. The same with Leclerc after the flat-spot. The idea of a multi-corner battle is dead with these racing regulations. All you have to do is dive super deep into the first in a series of corners and make the apex first, and suddenly, the bloke behind has no tools available to them. They either bail out, or in a vain attempt to hang around the outside, “cause” a collision when the defending car inevitably squeezes them off the road. That was the mistake Oscar made, instead of hanging around the outside and trying to overtake on track (god forbid!), he should’ve just skipped the corner like everyone else usually does and fired off down the road to try make up the five seconds! Never mind the ridiculous redesign of this track made before it returned to F1 a decade ago that made every corner into a tighter version of itself that reduces the number of viable lines and makes passing that much more difficult. So many outright anti-motor racing decisions being made in Formula 1 right now. Alianora La Canta (@alianora-la-canta) 2nd November 2026, 11:23 @thexrod In fact, if you dive super deep into the first corner, and your opponent is outside of you, then your opponent is then blamed and penalised for anything that ensues. This appears to have happened at least twice this race, and it’s not the first times this year. (The Oscar Piastri case for me was more to do with Oscar attempting to make it “multi-corner” than anything else, which makes it especially germane to this point). Roger Ayles (@roger-ayles) 2nd November 2026, 2:32 The anti-racing overly bloated no room for common sense rulebook strikes again. Piastri may not have been ‘fully’ alongside at whatever point of the apex they look at but he was basically halfway alongside and therefore not only had a right to place his car there but also had a right to be given room and to continue the overtaking attempt into T2. The rules basically saying that because he wasn’t alongside the other cars mirror at the apex he no longer had a right to continue the overtaking attempt and even saying he should have left the track is yet more proof that these anti-racing regulations aren’t fit for purpose. The guidelines simply don’t suit situations like this. Sure if your not mostly alongside someone on the outside of say the Monaco hairpin then the overtaking attempt isn’t on. But if your even a bit alongside on the outside of a corner that leads into another where you’ll then be on the inside then the overtaking attempt is still very much on. I’m so sick of this nonsense now and going back and watching racing from not only other categories but also past decades of F1 just makes me even more sick of the joke guidelines F1 has now! Setting up an overtake by placing your car on the outside of the other car, thus compromising their line into the corner, then benefiting from it in the next corner, should be a legitimate maneuver in a race. The other car may or may not leave you enough space going into the corner – but you cannot predict that in advance. So, in the absence of mind-reading capabilities, your choice is either to expect being given room and continue with the maneuver; or expect to be squeezed out and automatically back out of the attempt. But if the latter is the required behaviour as per the rulebook (unless you are fully alongside), because it is you who’ll get penalized if the other driver ignores your physical presence on track , then the rulebook makes a legitimate motor racing maneuver practically impossible to carry out. Riker (@corsair) 2nd November 2026, 3:27 So…they expected.PIA to go off the track to avoid the collision when half good car was already off the track at the time? Really? No way is that a 10s penalty. Sigh. Riker (@corsair) 2nd November 2026, 3:28 Meant to say “half the car”. Silly auto correct. Leaving the track was literally the only way for him to avoid contact, while Lindblad could’ve avoided the contact by using more of the track width he had available. Alianora La Canta (@alianora-la-canta) 2nd November 2026, 11:25 @corsair Yes. Apparently breaking the regulations is required to keep them. Juan Fanger (@juanfanger) 2nd November 2026, 5:30 David (@nvherman) 2nd November 2026, 7:16 Interesting to me that when Norris attempted to go around the outside of Leclerc at turn 5, no collision occurred. Yet again Piastri is involved in a collision because he doesn’t back out when the move isn’t on. Alianora La Canta (@alianora-la-canta) 2nd November 2026, 11:28 @nvherman Interestingly, when Piastri did that to Leclerc at Spa earlier this year, no penalty was given to Piastri (and a few days later, the stewards claimed they should have penalised Leclerc. So the stewards’ stance in Spa likely led to Oscar thinking he was right to continue the fight in that moment in Mexico (if not afterwards). David (@nvherman) 2nd November 2026, 11:52 Interestingly, when Piastri did that to Leclerc at Spa earlier this year, no penalty was given to Piastri Thank you for reminding me of that incident. I’ve just rewatched it , and I believe that that was considered differently due to the contact happening in the braking zone (and Piastri was farther alongside in that incident, plus Leclerc was affected as regards to position or being able to continue). Linblad played stupid games and won a stupid prize. Ridiculous penalty, you can’t just kill racing through multiple corners like that I simply don’t comprehend the stewards’ argument, essentially claiming that Piastri should’ve left track limits to avoid contact, even though Lindblad could’ve equally avoided the contact by moving more to the right, which is what the stewards should point out rather than that Piastri could’ve moved more to the left, which itself is true, but would’ve required him to leave the track entirely, not to mention stewards typically want drivers to remain within track limits whenever possible & he could remain since he wasn’t forced off, so their argument is also contradictory. All in all, their verdicts & decisions on Leclerc, Russell, & Piastri were baffling. Alianora La Canta (@alianora-la-canta) 2nd November 2026, 11:50 I feel like this whole situation could have been avoided, had the stewards not changed their verdict on the Piastri/Leclerc collision at Spa (presumably without evidence, as the change from “racing incident” to “Leclerc’s fault” was not accompanied by a penalty). That prevented Oscar from learning the right lessons from that crash and applying them here. How do I issue the FIA a 10-second penalty? Derek Warwick was one of this races Stewards…. says everything really. Rooie Piet (@axel3304) 2nd November 2026, 9:12 Racing incident at most. Ridiculous penalty which can only be defended by pointing to a set of guidelines which is time and time again proven to be woefully inadequate for judging incidents like this. They’re so hell-bent on concistency by applying black-and-white rules on grey areas that common sense is thrown out the window when judging an incident. Embarrassing. What are they supposed to do though? You complain that they shouldn’t apply black and white rules to a grey area, but then complain about bias or unequal treatment if they don’t then apply those same rules to every driver in a consistent way. Are they supposed to apply the rules equally to all, or are they meant to ignore the rules if it’s a more popular driver who ends up on the receiving end of that penalty? Is it really about “common sense”, or a sense of outrage that they dared to penalise Piastri when he’s more popular than Lindblad? Alianora La Canta (@alianora-la-canta) 2nd November 2026, 11:51 Unfortunately this approach means they also get accused of bias and inconsistency, since the stewards have demonstrably not been consistent between Piastri/Lindblad in Mexico and Piastri/Leclerc in Spa. Piastri’s penalty for colliding with Lindblad was…. …Given too late. Somehow F1 refereeing seems like a comitee having endless meetings about something that can be just straightforward. They should stop listening to the teams and drivers. And only judge the actions as they are. And if they cannot do that in reasonable time, they should spend some of those billions to make sure they can. Unless they can invent a time machine, that would be physically impossible regardless of how much was spent. If you can’t perform a task in a timely manner, you could: Improve the way of working Use better tools Hire more colleagues The FOM has their new operating centre for about a week. I’ll be curious to see if this will show in faster decision making. items.article_search_text: EXCLUSIVE: Oscar Piastri enjoyed great success before arriving into Formula 1, when his need to be independent was far greater than it is now, with the McLaren ace still having to adapt Oscar Piastri, like the majority of non-European natives, had to make notable sacrifices before his Formula 1 career took off and those challenges continue to shape who he is - for better and, occasionally, for worse. The Australian had arguably the greatest CV of any junior coming into the sport and has backed up that promise from day one. Upping sticks and moving halfway across the globe forced a young Piastri to adapt, to flourish independently. And whilst that delivered F2 and F3 titles, Piastri has confessed that the independence he relied upon for so long has become a habit he sometimes needs to let go of given the bundles of talent he has around him at McLaren. The British side have won successive Constructors' titles for the first time in 34 years as Zak Brown and co build a formidable outfit, spearheaded by Piastri and world champion Lando Norris. But the Australian concedes that sometimes he almost forgets how much assistance he can call upon given how long he had to take the lead by himself. He told Mirror Sport on his route into F1: "It definitely taught me a lot, I had to learn to do a lot of things myself and problem solve. In some ways that's definitely helped, but in other ways I almost rely on that independence too much. Especially in a team with so many people, I sometimes need reminding that I've got a lot of help to achieve what I want to achieve. "But in the grand scheme of things its definitely taught me a lot of life lessons and experiences that have been helpful. I think what the Aussies and anyone outside of Europe has is that shared experience of having to leave home and sacrifice something to go and chase our dreams." The ultimate dream of course being a world championship, which he came so close to last season. Piastri won seven races en route to finishing third in the standings, with the fight to be the sport's champion going down to the final race in Abu Dhabi. Not since 1980 have Australia boasted the world champion in F1, that being Alan Jones as he excelled in a Williams. Piastri looks to be their best hope since then and the McLaren ace would also relish the chance to deliver a victory Down Under, where success has been hard to come by for the natives. "Definitely towards the top," he said when quizzed on his ambitions of winning in Melbourne, his hometown. "I think a championship is the only thing above that, but it would be very cool to do that. Obviously we've not had a whole lot of success as Australians for a while now. For me even to step on the podium would be good first step, but to win it would be awesome." Piastri has sampled what it would be like to lap up the love of the crowd when he raced at Silverstone in 2023, which proved to be something of a watershed moment for the team, who had struggled massively for form before catapulting into the competitive outfit they are today. Norris qualified second, just ahead of Piastri. Come race day Norris would finish behind winner Max Verstappen , recording the team's first podium of the year. Piastri would come home in fourth, then his best finish in F1. And whilst the Australian expected Norris, not only a podium finisher, but also the home favourite, to get all the love when they went to greet the fans, he was taken a back to hear them chanting his name. He said: "Obviously having Lando as a teammate, who is a Brit, there's always the potential for it to be the Brits vs the Aussies but honestly one of my most memorable moments in F1 was when we raced there in 2023. "It was the first weekend when we were genuinely competitive and I remember we went to the fan stage after. I was a bit unlucky to miss out on a podium, but the fans chanted my name, and I wasn't expecting that at all. Lando had just finished on the podium and was the Brit in the team so it was really cool to experience that." F1's growth, especially over the last decade, has seen a new legion of fans take to the sport. That has seen the calendar grow, with it now boasting more races than ever and the appetite to attend races has reached new levels. This weekend in Mexico, which returned to the calendar in 2015 after a 23 year absence, will see Piastri look to secure a tenth win of his career, and his first this season, in a specially designed livery as McLaren partner with sponsor VELO. Piastri has said: "I think we have a great connection with our fans, and the best fanbase out there. "I've listened to Zak Brown deliver talks about many things, and one of the biggest things he wanted when he first joined was listening to the fans more and having them involved." VELO's Fandom campaign analysed the extent to with fans will go just to get to an F1 race with 1,000 people quizzed in the UK. One in five said they would reschedule their holiday if an opportunity came up to attend a race. Just over a quarter said they would bin off plans to celebrate their anniversary. Almost 40 percent confessed they had dodged a friend's birthday just to tune in to a race. Live Your Fandom is about celebrating the original and individual ways fans show up for the sport the love. The ‘Livery of Dreams’ brings that idea onto the F1 grid. Real fan dreams, turned into real life experiences, celebrated in an original design that can be seen across the McLaren car and wider race-weekend environment in Mexico.

Since Lando Norris missed out on victory in Madrid last month, McLaren have failed to finish on the podium in the last four races, despite bringing new parts to the car in that period. After qualifying eighth at last weekend's United States Grand Prix, Norris described the MCL40 as "easily the hardest car I've ever driven in my life". "There will be some more stuff coming," said team principal Andrea Stella on McLaren's upgrade plans, given most teams are now focusing on designing their 2027 cars. "I think ultimately we will only be able to do so across Brazil and Vegas. So, Mexico there won't be very much, but Brazil and Vegas there will be some upgrades. "Hopefully this will help us to be consistently in the fight for podiums and hopefully start to lean on the level of competitiveness that is required to fight for the victory. So, there's a few upgrades that are still in the pipeline." McLaren confirmed in their press release ahead of this weekend's Mexico City Grand Prix that the team "remains committed to learning, developing and extracting the maximum from the MCL40 at every opportunity". "After the successful introduction of changes to the front and rear corners of the MCL40 in Austin, the car will remain essentially unchanged going into this weekend's race," they added. "This will therefore only see a small selection of parts delivered to track in Mexico City through the team's development pathway with further developments in the pipeline for the remaining rounds of the 2026 season, starting from the race in Sao Paulo." Norris points to qualifying as a weakness Norris has claimed three pole positions this year in Budapest, Zandvoort and Madrid, but his biggest margin to second place in those qualifying sessions was 0.102s. The car appears to have been on a knife edge throughout the season, which Piastri has struggled more with, and Norris says the slow-speed corners have also been an issue for the team. "There's been a lot of races we have shone and done a very good job. Qualifyings we have struggled," Norris told Sky Sports F1 . "We roughly know where we need to improve the car. I think in Austin it was clear the slow-speed corners we lost almost three tenths a lap, every single lap. That's a chunky bit of lap time to lose so consistently. "We need to improve in certain areas. If we can do that, I'm very confident we can have some good results but it seems to be a challenging area for us to improve as much as we like. "We will keep working hard. The team are doing a very good job and we will keep trying to pick away." items.article_search_text: Oscar Piastri knows that being willing to change things up can often lead to something better. He backed himself to make the switch to McLaren in 2022, and it paid off. That belief has driven his partnership with Google Pixel from day one, and in chapter three, independent creative agency Emotive shows what life looks Shot with production partner Somesuch, the work supports the launch of Google’s newest flagship smartphone – Pixel 11 Pro – and reunites director Isaac Lock with the team behind chapter one. The idea plays on a truth about Oscar. His schedule is packed. Every moment is accounted for. Every second is optimised. So Pixel 11 sweats the small stuff, leaving Oscar free to sweat the big stuff – like his intense training regime. The hero film is the first of a number of social-first assets, with the rest rolling out across Google Pixel and Oscar’s social channels. Each chapter has built on the last. Chapter one saw Oscar make the switch to Pixel, playing on his famously understated personality to show that refusing to settle leads to something better. Chapter two handed the work to his fans, turning a social vote into the ‘Pastry PiasTee’, a t-shirt Oscar wore at the Canadian Grand Prix and now sold as official merchandise. Chapter three shows the payoff, bringing Google Pixel’s global platform, ‘Ask more of your phone’, to life in the world’s most glamorous racing postcode. As with every chapter, the work was made for social first, designed to entertain like native content. Says Emma Dodd, Head of Devices & Services Marketing, Google AUNZ: “We’re excited to showcase how helpful and powerful our latest suite of Pixel 11 devices can be for Australians when they have access to Gemini Intelligence right in the palm of their hand. It was a pleasure to continue our partnership with Oscar to bring this chapter of work to life.” Says Rupert Taylor, Senior Creative Director, Emotive: “After the success of the first two chapters, we wanted to take a look at Oscar’s world post switch. We also wanted to stay true to his deadpan comedic stylings, and make some well crafted content that works well in the feed.” Says Isaac Lock, Director, Somesuch: “I always relish the challenge of creating a funny and engaging performance with someone who isn’t an actor, but Oscar makes it easy. items.article_search_text: Sky Sports F1s Martin Brundle gives his verdict on Kimi Antonellis outstanding performance which puts him on the brink of becoming F1s youngest world champion and the struggles for McLarens Oscar Piastri and Mercedes George Russell Given that Red Bull and Ferrari, and from time to time McLaren, have undoubtedly closed down the pace advantage enjoyed by Mercedes in the first half of the season, it was looking possible that Kimi Antonelli might win the World Championship perhaps not fully in the style he would have wanted. His Austin qualifying and race performances demolished that concern in the most comprehensive way. From seemingly nowhere, he produced a stormer of an initial time in the third and final top-10 shootout to secure pole position and deny Max Verstappen's Red Bull and the two Ferraris of Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton, all of whom had seemed likely to beat him. It was his seventh pole of the season but his first since Spa back in the summer eight races ago, and therefore very timely. Latest Sky Sports deals or stream F1 with no contract 📺 Antonelli was 'simply outstanding' Kimi produced a perfect start and opening lap to comfortably lead, while the slow-starting Verstappen had to fend off the Ferraris. His pace, consistency, and tyre management thereafter was simply outstanding. Both Red Bull drivers, Verstappen and Isack Hadjar, had impressively made it through to Q3 having used only one set of soft tyres up to that point. This would give Max on the front row two brand new sets of soft tyres for the race, surely a significant advantage? As it turns out, not so, as they didn't last particularly well, forcing Max to pit first of everyone on Lap 13 of 56, and clearly now on a two-stop strategy. Mercedes didn't panic or respond, they trusted their data and instincts, and their championship-leading driver, to babysit his tyres at sufficient pace to make only one pit stop on Lap 24. With fresh tyres Max was inevitably very fast, and it initially appeared that he would be able to make up the extra 20 seconds he must spend in the pitlane for his second stop on Lap 31. But he couldn't clear the traffic with much ease. With his radio failing for the second time, but not before he would castigate his team for not moving his team-mate on a different run plan out of the way much sooner, he ended up a fairly disgruntled third. I did the post-race interviews and Max did though beam a nice smile when I complimented him on his overtake of Lando Norris up into Turn 1. It was pure Verstappen, just as he looked highly likely to lose a position to Leclerc, he converted that into an overtake of the McLaren with a stunning and controlled slice while extremely late on the brakes. It didn't do him much good in the end though because after Leclerc's own first stop on Lap 15, and having already been awesome on the opening lap of the race, he was mighty fast all the way to the chequered flag for a very well-earned second place. Ferrari had led all three practice sessions and so their qualifying had been a relative disappointment, but Hamilton too was rapid in the closing stages and would finish fourth just a second behind Verstappen. Another lap and he'd have joined his team-mate Leclerc on the podium. Norris did a fine job in fifth, having pitted on Lap 16 but then changing to a one-stopper, stretching his hard compound tyres a full 40 laps. In the end, he ran out of grip and slipped from second place, but it was good while it lasted. Piastri struggling with 2026 cars and Russell's 'harsh' penalty Oscar Piastri in the sister McLaren had another disappointing race, lacking front-running pace from relatively early on and finishing 52 seconds behind the winner. Oscar simply can't seem to gel with the 2026 cars and it's painful to witness after his stellar run last year. Piastri's struggles would heavily impact another driver having a season to forget in the shape of George Russell. On the opening lap Russell was both attacking Hadjar's slow-starting Red Bull and defending from Piastri. He ran wide at the Turn 12 hairpin at the end of the back straight and rejoined, marginally ahead of Piastri. The Stewards looked at all the camera angles and data and decided that Russell had gained a lasting advantage off the track by not losing a place to Piastri, but given it was the opening lap and the proximity of other cars, they served him half the normal 10-second penalty in mitigation. I thought that was harsh, George felt somewhat more strongly about it. Taking his five-second penalty at the first pit stop put him behind Piastri, and despite very solid initial pace on fresh tyres he simply couldn't find a way past the young Aussie and finished a full 54 seconds behind his winning team-mate in eighth place. Ouch. Another 11th for Audi! Liam Lawson drove very well again for two points at Racing Bulls in ninth and Pierre Gasly grabbed the final point for Alpine in 10th, the position he started. Nico Hulkenberg finished 11th and just out of the points - that's Audi's 10th race this year when just missing out. That's a torment which revives bad memories for me, back when points only went down to sixth place, I had a spate of dragging some reluctant machine past all the accidents and unreliability to finish a point-less seventh. Antonelli's supreme victory ensures he will be the youngest ever F1 world champion by over three years, usurping Sebastian Vettel. And the first Italian F1 world champion since Alberto Ascari in 1953, despite such motorsport passion and history in that country. Verstappen is now out of championship contention, incredibly for the first time since 2020. Russell and Hamilton would have to win every race until the end of the year, with Antonelli not showing up, for them to be champion. It's a case of when, and not if. Austin put on at great show at COTA, a combined 460,000 fans had all the usual great views along with live music, fun fairs, and many other attractions, and a spectacular hospitality suite and infinity pool at the very top of the already high first corner. The lucky few were transported over the track in gondolas on ski-slope-style pylons and cables, I'm impressed by how F1 keeps developing as a full experience, even though the race didn't turn out to be a classic.
